entries.e34a5ef4dddc4a21602d38eec4a7e38909443130: <div sID="gen32451" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="6" osisID="1Tim.6" sID="1Tim.6"/> <div eID="gen32451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32452" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32453" type="x-p"/> I. He treats of the duty of servants, <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.1-1Tim.6.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. Of false teachers, <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.3-1Tim.6.5">ver. 3-5</reference>. III. Of godliness and covetousness, <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.6-1Tim.6.10">ver. 6-10</reference>. IV. What Timothy was to flee, and what to follow, <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.11-1Tim.6.12">ver. 11, 12</reference>. V. A solemn charge, <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.13-1Tim.6.16">ver. 13-16</reference>. VI. A charge for the rich, <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.17-1Tim.6.19">ver. 17-19</reference>. And lastly, a charge to Timothy, <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.20-1Tim.6.21">ver. 20, 21</reference>.
entries.3556dfbc2f073a36aa2ba54ee66c0e302332ada2: <div eID="gen32453" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32452" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Duty of Servants. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 64.)</title> <div sID="gen32454" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Let as many servants as are under the yoke count their own masters worthy of all honour, that the name of God and <hi type="italic">his</hi> doctrine be not blasphemed. <hi type="super">2</hi> And they that have believing masters, let them not despise <hi type="italic">them,</hi> because they are brethren; but rather do <hi type="italic">them</hi> service, because they are faithful and beloved, partakers of the benefit. These things teach and exhort. <hi type="super">3</hi> If any man teach otherwise, and consent not to wholesome words, <hi type="italic">even</hi> the words of our Lord Jesus Christ, and to the doctrine which is according to godliness; <hi type="super">4</hi> He is proud, knowing nothing, but doting about questions and strifes of words, whereof cometh envy, strife, railings, evil surmisings, <hi type="super">5</hi> Perverse disputings of men of corrupt minds, and destitute of the truth, supposing that gain is godliness: from such withdraw thyself. <div eID="gen32454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32455" type="x-p"/> I. Here is the duty of servants. The apostle had spoken before of church-relations, here of our family-relations. Servants are here said to be <hi type="italic">under the yoke,</hi> which denotes both subjection and labour; they are yoked to work, not to be idle. If Christianity finds servants under the yoke, it continues them under it; for the gospel does not cancel the obligations any lie under either by the law of nature or by mutual consent. They must respect their masters, <hi type="italic">count them worthy of all honour</hi> (because they are their masters), of all the respect, observance, compliance, and obedience, that are justly expected from servants to their masters. Not that they were to think that of them which they were not; but as their masters they must count them worthy of all that honour which was fit for them to receive, <hi type="italic">that the name of God be not blasphemed.</hi> If servants that embraced the Christian religion should grow insolent and disobedient to their masters, the doctrine of Christ would be reflected on for their sakes, as if it had made men worse livers than they had been before they received the gospel. Observe, If the professors of religion misbehave themselves, <hi type="italic">the name of God and his doctrine</hi> are in danger of being blasphemed by those who seek occasion <hi type="italic">to speak evil of that worthy name by which we are called.</hi> And this is a good reason why we should all conduct ourselves well, that we may prevent the occasion which many seek, and will be very apt to lay hold of, to speak ill of religion for our sakes. Or suppose the master were a Christian, and a believer, and the servant a believer too, would not this excuse him, because <hi type="italic">in Christ there is neither bond nor free?</hi> No, by no means, for Jesus Christ did not come to dissolve the bond of civil relation, but to strengthen it: <hi type="italic">Those that have believing masters, let them not despise them because they are brethren;</hi> for this brotherhood relates only to spiritual privileges, not to any outward dignity or advantage (those misunderstood and abuse their religion who make it a pretence for denying the duties that they owe to their relations); nay, <hi type="italic">rather do them service, because they are faithful and beloved.</hi> They must think themselves the more obliged to serve them because the faith and love that bespeak men Christians oblige them to do good; and that is all wherein their service consists. Observe, It is a great encouragement to us in doing our duty to our relations if we have reason to think they are faithful and beloved, <hi type="italic">and partakers of the benefit,</hi> that is, of the benefit of Christianity. Again, Believing masters and servants are brethren, and partakers of the benefit; for in Christ Jesus there is neither bond nor free, for you are all one in Christ Jesus, <reference osisRef="Gal.3.28">Gal. iii. 28</reference>. Timothy is appointed to <hi type="italic">teach and exhort these things.</hi> Ministers must preach not only the general duties of all, but the duties of particular relations. <div eID="gen32455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32456" type="x-p"/> II. Paul here warns Timothy to withdraw from those who corrupted the doctrine of Christ, and made it the subject off strife, debate, and controversy: <hi type="italic">If any man teach otherwise</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.3-1Tim.6.5">v. 3-5</reference>), do not preach practically, do not teach and exhort that which is for the promoting of serious godliness—if he will not consent to wholesome words, words that have a direct tendency to heal the soul—if he will <hi type="italic">not consent</hi> to these, even the <hi type="italic">words of our Lord Jesus Christ.</hi> Observe, We are not required to consent to any words as wholesome words except the words of our Lord Jesus Christ; but to those we must give our unfeigned assent and consent, and <hi type="italic">to the doctrine which is according to godliness.</hi> Observe, The doctrine of our Lord Jesus is a doctrine according to godliness; it has a direct tendency to make people godly. But he that does not consent to the words of Christ <hi type="italic">is proud</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.4">v. 4</reference>) and contentious, ignorant, and does a great deal of mischief to the church, knowing nothing. Observe, Commonly those are most proud who know least; for with all their knowledge they do not know themselves.—<hi type="italic">But doting about questions.</hi> Those who fall off from the plain practical doctrines of Christianity fall in with controversies, which eat out the life and power of religion; they dote about questions <hi type="italic">and strifes of words,</hi> which do a great deal of mischief in the church, are the occasion of <hi type="italic">envy, strife, railings, evil surmisings.</hi> When men are not content with the words of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the doctrine which is according to godliness, but will frame notions of their own and impose them, and that too in their own words, which man's wisdom teaches, and not in the words which the Holy Ghost teaches (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.13">1 Cor. ii. 13</reference>), they sow the seeds of all mischief in the church. Hence come <hi type="italic">perverse disputings of men of corrupt minds</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.5">v. 5</reference>), disputes that are all subtlety, and no solidity. Observe, Men of corrupt minds are <hi type="italic">destitute of the truth.</hi> The reason why men's minds are corrupt is because they do not stick to <hi type="italic">the truth as it is in Jesus: supposing that gain is godliness,</hi> making religion truckle to their secular interest. From such as these Timothy is warned to withdraw himself. We observe, 1. The words of our Lord Jesus Christ are wholesome words, they are the fittest to prevent or heal the church's wounds, as well as to heal a wounded conscience; for Christ has the tongue of the learned, to speak a word in season to him that is weary, <reference osisRef="Isa.50.4">Isa. l. 4</reference>. The words of Christ are the best to prevent ruptures in the church; for none who profess faith in him will dispute the aptness or authority of his words who is their Lord and teacher, and it has never gone well with the church since the words of men have claimed a regard equal to his words, and in some cases a much greater. 2. Whoever teaches otherwise, and does not consent to these wholesome words, he is proud, knowing nothing; for pride and ignorance commonly go together. 3. Paul sets a brand only on those who consent not to the words of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the doctrine which is according to godliness; they are proud, knowing nothing: other words more wholesome he knew not. 4. We learn the sad effects of doting about questions and strifes of words; of such doting about questions comes envy, strife, evil surmisings, and perverse disputings; when men leave the wholesome words of our Lord Jesus Christ, they will never agree in other words, either of their own or other men's invention, but will perpetually wrangle and quarrel about them; and this will produce envy, when they see the words of others preferred to those they have adopted for their own; and this will be attended with jealousies and suspicions of one another, called here <hi type="italic">evil surmisings;</hi> then they will proceed to perverse disputings. 5. Such persons as are given to perverse disputings appear to be men of corrupt minds, and destitute of the truth; especially such as act in this manner for the sake of gain, which is all their godliness, supposing gain to be godliness, contrary to the apostle's judgment, who reckoned godliness great gain. 6. Good ministers and Christians will withdraw themselves from such. "Come out from among them, my people, and be ye separate," says the Lord: <hi type="italic">from such withdraw thyself.</hi>
entries.5935e4047317a33a362c6ccb25fff47c54eb2960: <div eID="gen32456" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Excellence of Contentment; Evil of Covetousness. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 64.)</title> <div sID="gen32457" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> But godliness with contentment is great gain. 7 For we brought nothing into <hi type="italic">this</hi> world, <hi type="italic">and it is</hi> certain we can carry nothing out. <hi type="super">8</hi> And having food and raiment let us be therewith content. <hi type="super">9</hi> But they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and <hi type="italic">into</hi> many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition. <hi type="super">10</hi> For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows. <hi type="super">11</hi> But thou, O man of God, flee these things; and follow after righteousness, godliness, faith, love, patience, meekness. <hi type="super">12</hi> Fight the good fight of faith, lay hold on eternal life, whereunto thou art also called, and hast professed a good profession before many witnesses. <div eID="gen32457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32458" type="x-p"/> From the mention of the abuse which some put upon religion, making it to serve their secular advantages, the apostle, <div eID="gen32458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32459" type="x-p"/> I. Takes occasion to show the excellency of contentment and the evil of covetousness. <div eID="gen32459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32460" type="x-p"/> 1. The excellency of contentment, <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.6-1Tim.6.8">v. 6-8</reference>. Some account Christianity an advantageous profession for this world. In the sense they mean this is false; yet it is undoubtedly true that, though Christianity is the worst trade, it is the best calling in the world. Those that make a trade of it, merely to serve their turn for this world, will be disappointed, and find it a sorry trade; but those that mind it as their calling, and make a business of it, will find it a gainful calling, for it has the promise of the life that now is, as well as of that which is to come. <div eID="gen32460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32461" type="x-p"/> (1.) The truth he lays down is that <hi type="italic">godliness with contentment is great gain.</hi> Some read it, <hi type="italic">godliness with a competency;</hi> that is, if a man have but a little in this world, yet, if he have but enough to carry him through it, he needs desire no more, his godliness with that will be his great gain. <hi type="italic">For a little which a righteous man has is better than the riches of many wicked,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.37.16">Ps. xxxvii. 16</reference>. We read it, <hi type="italic">godliness with contentment;</hi> godliness is itself great gain, it is profitable to all things; and, wherever there is true godliness, there will be contentment; but those have arrived at the highest pitch of contentment with their godliness are certainly the easiest happiest people in this world. <hi type="italic">Godliness with contentment,</hi> that is, Christian contentment (content must come from principles of godliness) is great gain; it is all the wealth in the world. He that is godly is sure to be happy in another world; and if withal he do by contentment accommodate himself to his condition in this world he has enough. Here we have, [1.] A Christian's gain; it is godliness with contentment, this is the true way to gain, yea, it is gain itself. [2.] A Christian's gain is great: it is not like the little gain of worldlings, who are so fond of a little worldly advantage. [3.] Godliness is ever accompanied with contentment in a great or less degree; all truly godly people have learned with Paul, in whatever state they are, to be therewith content, <reference osisRef="Phil.4.11">Phil. iv. 11</reference>. They are content with what God allots for them, well knowing that this is best for them. Let us all then endeavour after godliness with contentment. <div eID="gen32461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32462" type="x-p"/> (2.) The reason he gives for it is, <hi type="italic">For we brought nothing with us into this world, and it is certain we can carry nothing out,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.7">v. 7</reference>. This is a reason why we should be content with a little. [1.] Because we can challenge nothing as a debt that is due to us, for we came naked into the world. Whatever we have had since, we are obliged to the providence of God for it; but he that gave may take what and when he pleases. We had our beings, our bodies, our lives (which are more than meat, and which are more than raiment), when we came into the world, though we came naked, and brought nothing with us; may we not then be content while our beings and lives are continued to us, though we have not every thing we would have? We brought nothing with us into this world, and yet God provided for us, care was taken of us, we have been fed all our lives long unto this day; and therefore, when we are reduced to the greatest straits, we cannot be poorer than when we came into this world, and yet then we were provided for; therefore let us trust in God for the remaining part of our pilgrimage. [2.] We shall carry nothing with us out of this world. A shroud, a coffin, and a grave, are all that the richest man in the world can have from his thousands. Therefore why should we covet much? Why should we not be content with a little, because, how much soever we have, we must leave it behind us? <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.15-Eccl.5.16">Eccl. v. 15, 16</reference>. <div eID="gen32462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32463" type="x-p"/> (3.) Hence he infers, <hi type="italic">having food and raiment, let us be therewith content,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.8">v. 8</reference>. Food and a <hi type="italic">covering,</hi> including habitation as well as raiment. Observe, If God give us the necessary supports of life, we ought to be content therewith, though we have not the ornaments and delights of it. If nature should be content with a little, grace should be content with less; though we have not dainty food, though we have not costly raiment, if we have but food and raiment convenient for us we ought to be content. This was Agur's prayer: <hi type="italic">Give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with food convenient for me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.30.8">Prov. xxx. 8</reference>. Here we see, [1.] The folly of placing our happiness in these things, when we did not bring any thing into this world with us, and we can carry nothing out. What will worldlings do when death shall strip them of their happiness and portion, and they must take an everlasting farewell of all these things, on which they have so much doted? They may say with poor Micah, <hi type="italic">You have taken away my gods; and what have I more?</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.18.24">Jud. xviii. 24</reference>. [2.] The necessaries of life are the hounds of a true Christian's desire, and with these he will endeavour to be content; his desires are not insatiable; no, a little, a few comforts of this life, will serve him, and these may hope to enjoy: <hi type="italic">Having food and raiment.</hi> <div eID="gen32463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32464" type="x-p"/> 2. The evil of covetousness. <hi type="italic">Those that will be rich</hi> (that set their hearts upon the wealth of this world, and are resolved right or wrong, they will have it), <hi type="italic">fall into temptation and a snare,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.9">v. 9</reference>. It is not said, those that are rich, but those that will be rich, that is, that place their happiness in worldly wealth, that covet it inordinately, and are eager and violent in the pursuit of it. Those that are such <hi type="italic">fall into temptation and a snare,</hi> unavoidably; for, when the devil sees which way their lusts carry them, he will soon bait his hook accordingly. He knew how fond Achan would be of a wedge of gold, and therefore laid that before him. They fall into <hi type="italic">many foolish and hurtful lusts.</hi> Observe, <div eID="gen32464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32465" type="x-p"/> (1.) The apostle supposes that, [1.] Some will be rich; that is, they are resolved upon it, nothing short of a great abundance will satisfy. [2.] Such will not be safe nor innocent, for they will be in danger of ruining themselves for ever; they fall into temptation, and a snare, &c. [3.] Worldly lusts are foolish and hurtful, for they drown men in destruction and perdition. [4.] It is good for us to consider the mischievousness of worldly fleshly lusts. They are foolish, and therefore we should be ashamed of them, hurtful, and therefore we should be afraid of them, especially considering to what degree they are hurtful, for they <hi type="italic">drown men in destruction and perdition.</hi> <div eID="gen32465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32466" type="x-p"/> (2.) The apostle affirms that <hi type="italic">the love of money is the root of all evil,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.10">v. 10</reference>. What sins will not men be drawn to by the love of money? Particularly this was at the bottom of the apostasy of many from the faith of Christ; while they coveted money, they <hi type="italic">erred from the faith,</hi> they quitted their Christianity, and <hi type="italic">pierced themselves through with many sorrows.</hi> Observe, [1.] What is the root of all evil; the love of money: people may have money, and yet not love it; but, if they love it inordinately, it will push them on to all evil. [2.] Covetous persons will quit the faith, if that be the way to get money: <hi type="italic">Which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith. Demas hath forsaken me, having loved this present world,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.10">2 Tim. iv. 10</reference>. For the world was dearer to him than Christianity. Observe, Those that err from the faith pierce themselves with many sorrows; those that depart from God do but treasure up sorrows for themselves. <div eID="gen32466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32467" type="x-p"/> II. Hence he takes occasion to caution Timothy, and to counsel him to keep in the way of God and his duty, and particularly to fulfil the trust reposed in him as a minister. He addresses himself to him as <hi type="italic">a man of God.</hi> Ministers are men of God, and ought to conduct themselves accordingly in every thing; they are men employed for God, devoted to his honour more immediately. The prophets under the Old Testament were called men of God. 1. He charges Timothy to take heed of the love of money, which had been so pernicious to many: <hi type="italic">Flee these things.</hi> It ill becomes any men, but especially men of God, to set their hearts upon the things of this world; men of God should be taken up with the things of God. 2. To arm him against the love of the world, he directs him to follow that which is good. <hi type="italic">Follow after righteousness, godliness, faith, love, patience, meekness:</hi> righteousness in his conversation towards men, godliness towards God, faith and love as living principles, to support him and carry him on in the practice both of righteousness and godliness. Those that follow after righteousness and godliness, from a principle of faith and love, have need to put on patience and meekness—patience to bear both the rebukes of Providence and the reproaches of men, and meekness wherewith to instruct gainsayers and pass by the affronts and injuries that are done us. Observe, It is not enough that men of God flee these things, but they must follow after what is directly contrary thereto. Further, What excellent persons men of God are who follow after righteousness! They are the excellent of the earth, and, being acceptable to God, they should be approved of men. 3. He exhorts him to do the part of a soldier: <hi type="italic">Fight the good fight of faith.</hi> Note, Those who will get to heaven must fight their way thither. There must be a conflict with corruption and temptations, and the opposition of the powers of darkness. Observe, It is a good fight, it is a good cause, and it will have a good issue. It is the fight of faith; we do not war after the flesh, for the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, <reference osisRef="2Cor.10.3-2Cor.10.4">2 Cor. x. 3, 4</reference>. He exhorts him to <hi type="italic">lay hold on eternal life.</hi> Observe, (1.) Eternal life is the crown proposed to us, for our encouragement to war, and to fight the good fight of faith, the good warfare. (2.) This we must lay hold on, as those that are afraid of coming short of it and losing it. Lay hold, and take heed of losing your hold. <hi type="italic">Hold fast that which thou hast, that no man take thy crown,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.3.11">Rev. iii. 11</reference>. (3.) We are called to the fight, and to lay hold on eternal life. (4.) The profession Timothy and all faithful ministers make before many witnesses is a good profession; for they profess and engage to fight the good fight of faith, and to lay hold on eternal life; their calling and their own profession oblige them to this.
entries.7493eb018ab881302e1576f05a9a06dfefbdbc77: <div eID="gen32467" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Apostle's Solemn Charge; Caution to Rich. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 64.)</title> <div sID="gen32468" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> I give thee charge in the sight of God, who quickeneth all things, and <hi type="italic">before</hi> Christ Jesus, who before Pontius Pilate witnessed a good confession; <hi type="super">14</hi> That thou keep <hi type="italic">this</hi> commandment without spot, unrebukeable, until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ: <hi type="super">15</hi> Which in his times he shall show, <hi type="italic">who is</hi> the blessed and only Potentate, the King of kings, and Lord of lords; <hi type="super">16</hi> Who only hath immortality, dwelling in the light which no man can approach unto; whom no man hath seen, nor can see: to whom <hi type="italic">be</hi> honour and power everlasting. Amen. <hi type="super">17</hi> Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy; 18 That they do good, that they be rich in good works, ready to distribute, willing to communicate; <hi type="super">19</hi> Laying up in store for themselves a good foundation against the time to come, that they may lay hold on eternal life. <hi type="super">20</hi> O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane <hi type="italic">and</hi> vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called: <hi type="super">21</hi> Which some professing have erred concerning the faith. Grace <hi type="italic">be</hi> with thee. Amen. <div eID="gen32468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32469" type="x-p"/> The apostle here charges Timothy <hi type="italic">to keep this commandment</hi> (that is, the whole work of his ministry, all the trust reposed in him, all the service expected from him) <hi type="italic">without spot, unrebukable;</hi> he must conduct himself so in his ministry that he might not lay himself open to any blame nor incur any blemish. What are the motives to move him to this? <div eID="gen32469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32470" type="x-p"/> I. He gives him a solemn charge: <hi type="italic">I give thee charge in the sight of God that thou do this.</hi> He charges him as he will answer it at the great day to that God whose eyes are upon us all, who sees what we are and what we do:—<hi type="italic">God, who quickens all things,</hi> who has life in himself and is the fountain of life. This should quicken us to the service of God that we serve a God who quickens all things. He charges him before Christ Jesus, to whom in a peculiar manner he stood related as a minister of his gospel: <hi type="italic">Who before Pontius Pilate witnessed a good confession.</hi> Observe, Christ died not only as a sacrifice, but as a martyr; and he witnessed a good confession when he was arraigned before Pilate, saying (<reference osisRef="John.18.36-John.18.37">John xviii. 36, 37</reference>), <hi type="italic">My kingdom is not of this world: I am come to bear witness unto the truth.</hi> That good confession of his before Pilate, <hi type="italic">My kingdom is not of this world,</hi> should be effectual to draw off all his followers, both ministers and people, from the love of this world. <div eID="gen32470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32471" type="x-p"/> II. He reminds him of the confession that he himself had made: <hi type="italic">Thou hast professed a good profession before many witnesses</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.12">v. 12</reference>), namely, when he was ordained by the laying on of the hands of the presbytery. The obligation of that was still upon him, and he must live up to that, and be quickened by that, to do the work of his ministry. <div eID="gen32471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32472" type="x-p"/> III. He reminds him of Christ's second coming: "<hi type="italic">Keep this commandment-until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ;</hi> keep it as long as thou live, till Christ come at death to give thee a discharge. Keep it with an eye to his second coming, when we must all give an account of the talents we have been entrusted with," <reference osisRef="Luke.16.2">Luke xvi. 2</reference>. Observe, The Lord Jesus Christ will appear, and it will be a glorious appearing, not like his first appearing in the days of his humiliation. Ministers should have an eye to this appearing of the Lord Jesus Christ in all their ministrations, and, till his appearing, they are to keep this commandment without spot, unrebukable. Mentioning the appearing of Christ, as one that loved it, Paul loves to speak of it, and loves to speak of him who shall then appear. The appearing of Christ is certain (<hi type="italic">he shall show it</hi>), but it is not for us to know the time and season of it, which the Father has kept in his own power: let this suffice us, that in time he will show it, in the time that he thinks fit for it. Observe, <div eID="gen32472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32473" type="x-p"/> 1. Concerning Christ and God the Father the apostle here speaks great things. (1.) That God is the only Potentate; the powers of earthly princes are all derived from him, and depend upon him. The powers that exist are ordained of God, <reference osisRef="Rom.13.1">Rom. xiii. 1</reference>. He is the only Potentate that is absolute and sovereign, and perfectly independent. (2.) He is the blessed and the only Potentate, infinitely happy, and nothing can in the least impair his happiness. (3.) He is King of kings, and Lord of lords. All the kings of the earth derive their power from him; he gave them their crowns, they hold them under him, and he has a sovereign dominion over them. This is Christ's title (<reference osisRef="Rev.19.16">Rev. xix. 16</reference>), <hi type="italic">upon his vesture and his thigh;</hi> for he has a name higher than the kings of the earth. (4.) He only has immortality. He only is immortal in himself, and has immortality as he is the fountain of it, for the immortality of angels and spirits derived from him. (5.) He dwells in inaccessible light, <hi type="italic">light which no man can approach unto:</hi> no man can get to heaven but those whom he is pleased to bring thither, and admit into his kingdom. (6.) He is invisible: <hi type="italic">Whom no man hath seen, nor can see.</hi> It is impossible that mortal eyes should bear the brightness of the divine glory. No man can see God and live. <div eID="gen32473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32474" type="x-p"/> 2. Having mentioned these glorious attributes, he concludes with a doxology: <hi type="italic">To him be honour and power everlasting. Amen.</hi> God having all power and honour to himself, it is our duty to ascribe all power and honour to him. (1.) What an evil is sin, when committed against such a God, the blessed and only Potentate! The evil of it rises in proportion to the dignity of him against whom it is committed. (2.) Great is his condescension, to take notice of such mean and vile creatures as we are. What are we then, that the blessed God, the King of kings and Lord of lords, should seek after us? (3.) Blessed are those who are admitted to dwell with this great and blessed Potentate. <hi type="italic">Happy are thy men</hi> (says the queen of Sheba to king Solomon), <hi type="italic">happy are these thy servants, who stand continually before thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.8">1 Kings x. 8</reference>. Much more happy are those who are allowed to stand before the King of kings. (4.) Let us love, adore, and praise, the great God; for <hi type="italic">who shall not fear thee, O Lord, and glorify thy name? For thou only art holy,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.15.4">Rev. xv. 4</reference>. <div eID="gen32474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32475" type="x-p"/> IV. The apostle adds, by way of postscript, a lesson for rich people, <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.17-1Tim.6.19">v. 17-19</reference>. <div eID="gen32475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32476" type="x-p"/> 1. Timothy must charge those that are rich to beware of the temptations, and improve the opportunities, of their prosperous estate. (1.) He must caution them to take heed of pride. This is a sin that easily besets rich people, upon whom the world smiles. Charge them <hi type="italic">that they be not high-minded,</hi> or think of themselves above what is meet, or be puffed up with their wealth. (2.) He must caution them against vain confidence in their wealth. Charge them that they <hi type="italic">trust not in uncertain riches.</hi> Nothing is more uncertain than the wealth of this world; many have had much of it one day and been stripped of all the next. Riches make themselves wings, and fly away as an eagle, &c., <reference osisRef="Prov.23.5">Prov. xxiii. 5</reference>. (3.) He must charge them to <hi type="italic">trust in God, the living God,</hi> to make him their hope, <hi type="italic">who giveth us richly all things to enjoy.</hi> Those who are rich must see God giving them their riches, and giving them to enjoy them richly; for many have riches, but enjoy them poorly, not having a heart to use them. (4.) He must charge them to do good with what they have (for what is the best estate worth, any more than as it gives a man an opportunity of doing so much the more good?): <hi type="italic">That they be rich in good works.</hi> Those are truly rich who are rich in good works. That they be <hi type="italic">ready to distribute, willing to communicate:</hi> not only to do it, but to do it willingly, for <hi type="italic">God loves a cheerful giver.</hi> (5.) He must charge them to think of another world, and prepare for that which is to come by works of charity: <hi type="italic">Laying up in store a good foundation against the time to come,</hi> that they may take hold on eternal life. <div eID="gen32476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32477" type="x-p"/> 2. Hence we may observe, (1.) Ministers must not be afraid of the rich; be they ever so rich, they must speak to them, and charge them. (2.) They must caution them against pride, and vain confidence in their riches: <hi type="italic">That they be not high-minded, nor trust in uncertain riches.</hi> Stir them up to works of piety and charity: <hi type="italic">That they do good,</hi> &c. (3.) This is the way for the rich to lay up in store for themselves for the time to come, that they may lay hold on eternal life; in the way of well-doing we are to seek for glory, honour, and immortality, <hi type="italic">and eternal life will be the end of all,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.2.7">Rom. ii. 7</reference>. (4.) Here is a lesson for ministers in the charge given to Timothy: <hi type="italic">Keep that which is committed to thy trust.</hi> Every minister is a trustee, and it is a treasure committed to his trust, which he has to keep. The truths of God, the ordinances of God, keep these, <hi type="italic">avoiding profane and vain babblings;</hi> not affecting human eloquence, which the apostle calls vain babbling, or human learning, which often opposes the truths of God, but keep close to the written word, for that is committed to our trust. Some who have been very proud of their learning, their <hi type="italic">science, which is falsely so called,</hi> have by that been debauched in their principles and been drawn away from the faith of Christ, which is a good reason why we should keep to the plain word of the gospel, and resolve to live and die by that. Observe, [1.] Ministers cannot be too earnestly exhorted to keep what is committed to their trust, because it is a great trust lodged with them: <hi type="italic">O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust!</hi> as if he had said, "I cannot conclude without charging thee again; whatever thou doest, be sure to keep this trust, for it is too great a trust to be betrayed." [2.] Ministers are to avoid babblings, if they would keep what is committed to them, because they are vain and profane. [3.] That science that opposes the truth of the gospel is falsely so called; it is not true science, for if it were it would approve of the gospel and consent to it. [4.] Those who are so fond of such science are in great danger of erring concerning the faith; those who are for advancing reason above faith are in danger of leaving faith. <div eID="gen32477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32478" type="x-p"/> V. Our apostle concludes with a solemn prayer and benediction: <hi type="italic">Grace be with thee. Amen.</hi> Observe, this is a short, yet comprehensive prayer for our friends, for grace comprehends in it all that is good, and grace is an earnest, yea, a beginning, of glory; for, wherever God gives grace, he will give glory, and will not withhold any good thing from him who walketh uprightly. Grace be with you all. Amen.  <chapter eID="1Tim.6"/> <div eID="gen32478" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen32351" osisID="1Tim" type="book"/>

entries.3cf5512e1834b7ae83e24ce6d531fdb06221803c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18147"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 6</title> <div sID="gen37423" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.1-1Tim.6.21">1Ti 6:1-21</reference>. Exhortations as to Distinctions of Civil Rank; the Duty of Slaves, in Opposition to the False Teachings of Gain-seekers; Timothy's Pursuit Is to Be Godliness, Which Is an Everlasting Possession: Solemn Adjuration to Do So against Christ's Coming; Charge to Be Given to the Rich. Concluding Exhortation.<div eID="gen37423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37424" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18147"/><hi type="bold">1. servants--</hi>to be taken as predicated thus, "Let as many as are under the yoke (as) slaves" (<reference osisRef="Titus.2.9">Tit 2:9</reference>). The exhortation is natural as there was a danger of Christian slaves inwardly feeling above their heathen masters.<div eID="gen37424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37425" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">their own masters--</hi>The phrase "their own," is an argument for submissiveness; it is not strangers, but their own masters whom they are required to respect.<div eID="gen37425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37426" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all honour--</hi>all possible and fitting honor; not merely outward subjection, but that inward honor from which will flow spontaneously right outward conduct (see on <reference osisRef="Eph.5.22">Ep 5:22</reference>).<div eID="gen37426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37427" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that the name of God--</hi>by which Christians are called.<div eID="gen37427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37428" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">blasphemed--</hi>Heathen masters would say, What kind of a God must be the God of the Christians, when such are the fruits of His worship (<reference osisRef="Rom.2.24">Ro 2:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.2.5">Tit 2:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.10">10</reference>)? <div eID="gen37428" type="x-p"/>
entries.f70794a2a416d050c3619c36e22ff94bfe04e43d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18148"/><div sID="gen37429" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18148"/><hi type="bold">2. And--</hi>rather, "But." The opposition is between those Christian slaves under the yoke of heathen, and those that have believing masters (he does not use the phrase "under the yoke" in the latter case, for service under believers is not a yoke). Connect the following words thus, "Let them (the slaves) not, because they (the masters) are brethren (and so equals, masters and slaves alike being Christians), despise them (the masters)."<div eID="gen37429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37430" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but rather, &c.--</hi>"but all the more (so much the more: with the greater good will) do them service because they (the masters) are faithful (that is, believers) and beloved who receive (in the mutual interchange of relative duties between master and servant; so the Greek) the benefit" (English Version violates Greek grammar). This latter clause is parallel to, "because they are brethren"; which proves that "they" refers to the masters, not the servants, as Tittmann takes it, explaining the verb in the common sense (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.54">Lu 1:54</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.20.35">Ac 20:35</reference>), "who sedulously labor for their (masters') benefit." The very term "benefit" delicately implies service done with the right motive, Christian "good will" (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.7">Ep 6:7</reference>). If the common sense of the Greek verb be urged, the sense must be, "Because they (the masters) are faithful and beloved who are sedulously intent on the benefiting" of their servants. But Porphyry [On Abstinence, 1.46] justifies the sense of the Greek verb given above, which also better accords with the context; for otherwise, the article "the," will have nothing in the preceding words to explain it, whereas in my explanation above "the benefit" will be that of the slaves' service.<div eID="gen37430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37431" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">These things teach--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Tim.4.11">1Ti 4:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.2.15">Tit 2:15</reference>). <div eID="gen37431" type="x-p"/>
entries.232379f7c9040da7db2c1ed60560e59845b1b6c0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18149"/><div sID="gen37432" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18149"/><hi type="bold">3. teach otherwise--</hi>than I desire thee to "teach" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.2">1Ti 6:2</reference>). The Greek indicative implies, he puts not a merely supposed case, but one actually existing, <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.3">1Ti 1:3</reference>, "Every one who teaches otherwise," that is, who teaches heterodoxy.<div eID="gen37432" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37433" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">consent not--</hi>Greek, "accede not to."<div eID="gen37433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37434" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wholesome--</hi>"sound" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.10">1Ti 1:10</reference>): opposed to the false teachers' words, unsound through profitless science and immorality.<div eID="gen37434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37435" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">words of our Lord Jesus Christ--</hi>Paul's inspired words are not merely his own, but are also Christ's words. <div eID="gen37435" type="x-p"/>
entries.3d3450ac942fa630b958c91c268e189834061f3d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18150"/><div sID="gen37436" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18150"/><hi type="bold">4. He is proud--</hi>literally, "wrapt in smoke"; filled with the fumes of self-conceit (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.6">1Ti 3:6</reference>) while "knowing nothing," namely, of the doctrine which is according to godliness (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.3">1Ti 6:3</reference>), though arrogating pre-eminent knowledge (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.7">1Ti 1:7</reference>).<div eID="gen37436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37437" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">doting about--</hi>literally, "sick about"; the opposite of "wholesome" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.3">1Ti 6:3</reference>). Truth is not the center about which his investigations move, but mere word-strifes.<div eID="gen37437" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37438" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">questions--</hi>of controversy.<div eID="gen37438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37439" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">strifes of words--</hi>rather than about realities (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.14">2Ti 2:14</reference>). These stand with them instead of "godliness" and "wholesome words" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.3">1Ti 6:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.4">1Ti 1:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.3.9">Tit 3:9</reference>).<div eID="gen37439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37440" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">evil surmisings--</hi>as to those who are of a different party from themselves. <div eID="gen37440" type="x-p"/>
entries.c48c6a817cf50e4de931285e4a06cff5f5b9e4ff: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18151"/><div sID="gen37441" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18151"/><hi type="bold">5. Perverse disputings--</hi>useless disputings. The oldest manuscripts read, "lasting contests" [Wiesinger]; "incessant collisions" [Alford]. "Strifes of words" had already been mentioned so that he would not be likely to repeat the same idea (as in the English Version reading) again.<div eID="gen37441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37442" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">corrupt minds--</hi>Greek, "of men corrupted (depraved) in mind." The inmost source of the evil is in the perverted mind (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.4">1Ti 6:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.8">2Ti 3:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.1.15">Tit 1:15</reference>).<div eID="gen37442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37443" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">destitute of the truth--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Titus.1.14">Tit 1:14</reference>). They had had the truth, but through want of moral integrity and of love of the truth, they were misled by a pretended deeper gnosis (knowledge) and higher ascetical holiness, of which they made a trade [Wiesinger].<div eID="gen37443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37444" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">supposing, &c.--</hi>The Greek requires, "supposing (regarding the matter in this point of view) that piety (so translated for 'godliness') is a means of gain (that is, a way of advancing one's worldly interests: a different Greek form, poriswa, expresses the thing gained, gain)"; not "that gain is godliness," as English Version.<div eID="gen37444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37445" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from such withdraw thyself--</hi>omitted in the oldest manuscripts. The connection with <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.6">1Ti 6:6</reference> favors the omission of these words, which interrupt the connection. <div eID="gen37445" type="x-p"/>
entries.1c541ee6769dbea94c6a75624d4ded51ecef2800: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18152"/><div sID="gen37446" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18152"/><hi type="bold">6. But--</hi>Though they err in this, there is a sense in which "piety is" not merely gain, but "great means of gain": not the gaining which they pursue, and which makes men to be discontented with their present possessions, and to use religion as "a cloak of covetousness" (<reference osisRef="1Thess.2.5">1Th 2:5</reference>) and means of earthly gain, but the present and eternal gain which piety, whose accompaniment is contentment, secures to the soul. Wiesinger remarks that Paul observed in Timothy a tendency to indolence and shrinking from the conflict, whence he felt (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.11">1Ti 6:11</reference>) that Timothy needed cautioning against such temptation; compare also the second Epistle. Not merely contentment is great gain (a sentiment of the heathen Cicero [Paradox 6], "the greatest and surest riches"), but "piety with contentment"; for piety not only feels no need of what it has not, but also has that which exalts it above what it has not [Wiesinger]. The Greek for contentment is translated "sufficiency" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.9.8">2Co 9:8</reference>). But the adjective (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.11">Php 4:11</reference>) "content"; literally, "having a sufficiency in one's self" independent of others. "The Lord always supplies His people with what is necessary for them. True happiness lies in piety, but this sufficiency [supplied by God, with which moreover His people are content] is thrown into the scale as a kind of overweight" [Calvin] (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.17.1-1Kgs.17.16">1Ki 17:1-16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.37.19">Psa 37:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.33.6">Is 33:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.16">16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.37.21">Jr 37:21</reference>). <div eID="gen37446" type="x-p"/>
entries.b6d5a36e39ad3b8507fbd5ec6f9ea7592de4ac36: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18153"/><div sID="gen37447" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18153"/><hi type="bold">7. For--</hi>confirming the reasonableness of "contentment."<div eID="gen37447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37448" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and it is certain--</hi>Vulgate and other old versions support this reading. The oldest manuscripts, however, omit "and it is certain"; then the translation will be, "We brought nothing into the world (to teach us to remember) that neither can we carry anything out" (<reference osisRef="Job.1.21">Job 1:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.15">Ec 5:15</reference>). Therefore, we should have no gain-seeking anxiety, the breeder of discontent (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.25">Mt 6:25</reference>). <div eID="gen37448" type="x-p"/>
entries.5b49c287b908b931a1f588228b7f0186b9c9f65e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18154"/><div sID="gen37449" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18154"/><hi type="bold">8. And--</hi>Greek, "But." In contrast to the greedy gain-seekers (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.5">1Ti 6:5</reference>).<div eID="gen37449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37450" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">having--</hi>so long as we have food. (The Greek expresses "food sufficient in each case for our continually recurring wants" [Alford]). It is implied that we, as believers, shall have this (<reference osisRef="Isa.23.16">Is 23:16</reference>).<div eID="gen37450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37451" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">raiment--</hi>Greek, "covering"; according to some including a roof to cover us, that is, a dwelling, as well as clothing.<div eID="gen37451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37452" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">let us be therewith content--</hi>literally, "we shall be sufficiently provided"; "we shall be sufficed" [Alford]. <div eID="gen37452" type="x-p"/>
entries.ca7d3bb190b4af9c5a178fe871e610c08501fdc8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18155"/><div sID="gen37453" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18155"/><hi type="bold">9. will be rich--</hi>have more than "food and raiment." Greek, "wish to be rich"; not merely are willing, but are resolved, and earnestly desire to have riches at any cost (<reference osisRef="Prov.28.20">Pr 28:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.28.22">22</reference>). This wishing (not the riches themselves) is fatal to "contentment" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.6">1Ti 6:6</reference>). Rich men are not told to cast away their riches, but not to "trust" in them, and to "do good" with them (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.17">1Ti 6:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.18">18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.62.10">Psa 62:10</reference>).<div eID="gen37453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37454" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fall into temptation--</hi>not merely "are exposed to temptation," but actually "fall into" it. The falling into it is what we are to pray against, "Lead us not into temptation" (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.14">Jas 1:14</reference>); such a one is already in a sinful state, even before any overt act of sin. The Greek for "temptation" and "gain" contains a play on sounds--porasmus, peirasmus.<div eID="gen37454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37455" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">snare--</hi>a further step downwards (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.7">1Ti 3:7</reference>). He falls into "the snare of the devil."<div eID="gen37455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37456" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">foolish--</hi>irrational.<div eID="gen37456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37457" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hurtful--</hi>to those who fall into the snare. Compare <reference osisRef="Eph.4.22">Ep 4:22</reference>, "deceitful lusts" which deceive to one's deadly hurt.<div eID="gen37457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37458" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lusts--</hi>With the one evil lust ("wish to be rich") many others join themselves: the one is the "root of all evils" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.10">1Ti 6:10</reference>).<div eID="gen37458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37459" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which--</hi>Greek, "whatever (lusts)."<div eID="gen37459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37460" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">drown--</hi>an awful descending climax from "fall into"; this is the last step in the terrible descent (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.15">Jas 1:15</reference>); translated "sink," <reference osisRef="Luke.5.7">Lu 5:7</reference>.<div eID="gen37460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37461" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">destruction ... perdition--</hi>destruction in general (temporal or eternal), and perdition in particular, namely, that of body and soul in hell. <div eID="gen37461" type="x-p"/>
entries.17214b721a83a4708006930cc80d5f8a46b87985: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18156"/><div sID="gen37462" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18156"/><hi type="bold">10. the love of money--</hi>not the money itself, but the love of it--the wishing to be rich (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.9">1Ti 6:9</reference>)--"is a root (Ellicott and Middleton: not as English Version, 'the root') of all evils." (So the Greek plural). The wealthiest may be rich not in a bad sense; the poorest may covet to be so (<reference osisRef="Ps.62.10">Psa 62:10</reference>). Love of money is not the sole root of evils, but it is a leading "root of bitterness" (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.15">He 12:15</reference>), for "it destroys faith, the root of all that is good" [Bengel]; its offshoots are "temptation, a snare, lusts, destruction, perdition."<div eID="gen37462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37463" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">coveted after--</hi>lusted after.<div eID="gen37463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37464" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">erred from--</hi>literally, "have been made to err from the faith" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.19">1Ti 1:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.1">4:1</reference>).<div eID="gen37464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37465" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pierced--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Luke.2.35">Lu 2:35</reference>).<div eID="gen37465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37466" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with ... sorrows--</hi>"pains": "thorns" of the parable (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.22">Mt 13:22</reference>) which choke the word of "faith." "The prosperity of fools destroys them" (<reference osisRef="Prov.1.32">Pr 1:32</reference>). Bengel and Wiesinger make them the gnawings of conscience, producing remorse for wealth badly acquired; the harbingers of the future "perdition" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.9">1Ti 6:9</reference>). <div eID="gen37466" type="x-p"/>
entries.12cfd21862f40a0cadd8b4d2e624b4f132231c44: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18157"/><div sID="gen37467" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18157"/><hi type="bold">11. But thou--</hi>in contrast to the "some" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.10">1Ti 6:10</reference>).<div eID="gen37467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37468" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">man of God--</hi>who hast God as thy true riches (<reference osisRef="Gen.15.1">Ge 15:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.16.5">Psa 16:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.3.24">La 3:24</reference>). Applying primarily to Timothy as a minister (compare <reference osisRef="2Pet.1.21">2Pe 1:21</reference>), just as the term was used of Moses (<reference osisRef="Deut.33.1">De 33:1</reference>), Samuel (<reference osisRef="1Sam.9.6">1Sa 9:6</reference>), Elijah, and Elisha; but, as the exhortation is as to duties incumbent also on all Christians, the term applies secondarily to him (so <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.17">2Ti 3:17</reference>) as a Christian man born of God (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.18">Jas 1:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.5.1">1Jo 5:1</reference>), no longer a man of the world raised above earthly things; therefore, God's property, not his own, bought with a price, and so having parted with all right in himself: Christ's work is to be his great work: he is to be Christ's living representative.<div eID="gen37468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37469" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">flee these things--</hi>namely, "the love of money" with its evil results (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.9">1Ti 6:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.10">10</reference>).<div eID="gen37469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37470" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">follow after righteousness--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.22">2Ti 2:22</reference>).<div eID="gen37470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37471" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">godliness--</hi>"piety." Righteousness is more in relation to our fellow man; piety ("godliness") to God"; faith is the root of both (see on <reference osisRef="Titus.2.12">Tit 2:12</reference>).<div eID="gen37471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37472" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">love--</hi>by which "faith worketh."<div eID="gen37472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37473" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">patience--</hi>enduring perseverance amidst trials.<div eID="gen37473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37474" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">meekness--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read, "meek-spiritedness," namely, towards the opponents of the Gospel. <div eID="gen37474" type="x-p"/>
entries.66247d8f3c3a7497eb7a17eda334af661dd7245d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18158"/><div sID="gen37475" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18158"/><hi type="bold">12. Fight the good fight--</hi>Birks thinks this Epistle was written from Corinth, where contests in the national games recurred at stated seasons, which will account for the allusion here as in <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.24-1Cor.9.26">1Co 9:24-26</reference>. Contrast "strifes of words" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.4">1Ti 6:4</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.18">1Ti 1:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.7">2Ti 4:7</reference>. The "good profession" is connected with the good fight (<reference osisRef="Ps.60.4">Psa 60:4</reference>).<div eID="gen37475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37476" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lay hold on eternal life--</hi>the crown, or garland, the prize of victory, laid hold of by the winner in the "good fight" (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.7">2Ti 4:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.8">8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.3.12-Phil.3.14">Php 3:12-14</reference>). "Fight (literally, 'strive') with such striving earnestness as to lay hold on the prize, eternal life."<div eID="gen37476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37477" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">also--</hi>not in the oldest manuscripts.<div eID="gen37477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37478" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">professed a good profession--</hi>Greek, "didst confess THE good confession," namely, the Christian confession (as the Greek word is the same in this verse as that for "confession" in <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.13">1Ti 6:13</reference>, probably the profession here is the confession that Christ's kingdom is the kingdom of the truth, <reference osisRef="John.18.36">Joh 18:36</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.18.37">37</reference>), at thy being set apart to thy ministerial function (whether in general, or as overseer at Ephesus): the same occasion as is referred to in <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.18">1Ti 1:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.14">4:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.4">2Ti 1:4</reference>.<div eID="gen37478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37479" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">before many witnesses--</hi>who would testify against thee if thou shouldest fall away [Bengel]. <div eID="gen37479" type="x-p"/>
entries.73ebdffcb1b5476e7c42fcb623f0f7640e66369a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18159"/><div sID="gen37480" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18159"/><hi type="bold">13. quickeneth all things--</hi>that is, "maketh alive." But the oldest manuscripts read, "preserveth alive"; as the same Greek means in <reference osisRef="Acts.7.19">Ac 7:19</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Neh.9.6">Ne 9:6</reference>. He urges Timothy to faithfulness here by the present manifestation of God's power in preserving all things, as in <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.14">1Ti 6:14</reference>, by the future manifestation of God's power at the appearing of Christ. The assurance that "eternal life," <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.12">1Ti 6:12</reference>, will be the result of "fighting the good fight," rests on the fulness and power of Him who is the God of all life, present and to come.<div eID="gen37480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37481" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">witnessed--</hi>It was the Lord's part to witness, Timothy's part to confess (or "profess," <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.12">1Ti 6:12</reference>) "the good confession" [Bengel]. The confession was His testimony that He was King, and His kingdom that of the truth (see on <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.12">1Ti 6:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.15">1Ti 6:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.27.11">Mt 27:11</reference>). Christ, in attesting, or bearing witness to this truth, attested the truth of the whole of Christianity. Timothy's profession, or confession, included therefore the whole of the Christian truth. <div eID="gen37481" type="x-p"/>
entries.f61e5db0bc0a524952015202d8c41747352a30b5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18160"/><div sID="gen37482" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18160"/><hi type="bold">14. keep this commandment--</hi>Greek, "the commandment," that is, the Gospel rule of life (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.5">1Ti 1:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.13.34">Joh 13:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.21">2Pe 2:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.2">3:2</reference>).<div eID="gen37482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37483" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">without spot, unrebukeable--</hi>agreeing with "thou." Keep the commandment and so be without spot," &c. "Pure" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.22">1Ti 5:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.5.27">Ep 5:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.1.27">Jas 1:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.14">2Pe 3:14</reference>).<div eID="gen37483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37484" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">until the appearing of ... Christ--</hi>His coming in person (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.8">2Th 2:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.2.13">Tit 2:13</reference>). Believers then used in their practice to set before themselves the day of Christ as near at hand; we, the hour of death [Bengel]. The fact has in all ages of the Church been certain, the time as uncertain to Paul, as it is to us; hence, <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.15">1Ti 6:15</reference>, he says, "in His times": the Church's true attitude is that of continual expectation of her Lord's return (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.8">1Co 1:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.1.6">Php 1:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.10">10</reference>). <div eID="gen37484" type="x-p"/>
entries.fcc9f26b167b3298618e4e9aac865278b7714935: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18161"/><div sID="gen37485" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18161"/><hi type="bold">15. in his times--</hi>Greek, "His own [fitting] times" (<reference osisRef="Acts.1.7">Ac 1:7</reference>). The plural implies successive stages in the manifestation of the kingdom of God, each having its own appropriate time, the regulating principle and knowledge of which rests with the Father (<reference osisRef="1Tim.2.6">1Ti 2:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.9">2Ti 1:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.1.3">Tit 1:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.1.1">He 1:1</reference>).<div eID="gen37485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37486" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he shall show--</hi>"display": an expression appropriate in reference to His "APPEARING," which is stronger than His "coming," and implies its visibility; "manifest": make visible (compare <reference osisRef="Acts.3.20">Ac 3:20</reference>): "He" is the Father (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.16">1Ti 6:16</reference>).<div eID="gen37486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37487" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">blessed--</hi>in Himself: so about to be the source of blessing to His people at Christ appearing, whence flows their "blessed hope" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.11">1Ti 1:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.2.13">Tit 2:13</reference>).<div eID="gen37487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37488" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">only--</hi>(<reference osisRef="John.17.3">Joh 17:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.16.27">Ro 16:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.15.4">Re 15:4</reference>).<div eID="gen37488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37489" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">King of kings--</hi>elsewhere applied also to Jesus (<reference osisRef="Rev.1.5">Re 1:5</reference>; 17:14; 19:16). <div eID="gen37489" type="x-p"/>
entries.129658723574138f30796ab4645307fb8ae8f377: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18162"/><div sID="gen37490" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18162"/><hi type="bold">16. Who only hath immortality--</hi>in His own essence, not merely at the will of another, as all other immortal beings [Justin Martyr, Quæst. ad Orthod., 61]. As He hath immortality, so will He give it to us who believe; to be out of Him is death. It is mere heathen philosophy that attributes to the soul indestructibility in itself, which is to be attributed solely to God's gift. As He hath life in Himself, so hath He given to the Son to have life in Himself (<reference osisRef="John.5.26">Joh 5:26</reference>). The term used in the New Testament for "immortal," which does not occur, is "incorruptible." "Immortality" is found in <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.53">1Co 15:53</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.54">54</reference>.<div eID="gen37490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37491" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dwelling in the light which no man can approach unto--</hi>After life comes mention of light, as in <reference osisRef="John.1.4">Joh 1:4</reference>. That light is unapproachable to creatures, except in so far as they are admitted by Him, and as He goes forth to them [Bengel]. It is unapproachable on account of its exceeding brightness [Theophylact]. If one cannot gaze steadfastly at the sun, which is but a small part of creation, by reason of its exceeding heat and power, how much less can mortal man gaze at the inexpressible glory of God [Theophylact, To Autolycus] (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.2">Psa 104:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.1.5">1Jo 1:5</reference>).<div eID="gen37491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37492" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no man hath seen--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Exod.23.20">Ex 23:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.1.18">Joh 1:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.1.15">Col 1:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.11.27">He 11:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.4.12">1Jo 4:12</reference>). Perhaps even in the perfect state no creature shall fully see God. Still the saints shall, in some sense, have the blessedness of seeing Him, which is denied to mere man (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.8">Mt 5:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.13.12">1Co 13:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.3.2">1Jo 3:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.22.4">Re 22:4</reference>). <div eID="gen37492" type="x-p"/>
entries.d35e964811e08b0ea4fb6ac5694b6cb7fe395243: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18163"/><div sID="gen37493" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18163"/>17. Resuming the subject from above, <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.5">1Ti 6:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.10">10</reference>. The immortality of God, alone rich in glory, and of His people through Him, is opposed to the lust of money (compare <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.14-1Tim.6.16">1Ti 6:14-16</reference>). From speaking of the desire to be rich, he here passes to those who are rich: (1) What ought to be their disposition; (2) What use they ought to make of their riches, and, (3) The consequences of their so using them.<div eID="gen37493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37494" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rich in this world--</hi>contrasted with the riches of the future kingdom to be the portion of believers at Christ's "appearing," <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.14">1Ti 6:14</reference>.<div eID="gen37494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37495" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">high-minded--</hi>often the character of the rich (see <reference osisRef="Rom.12.16">Ro 12:16</reference>).<div eID="gen37495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37496" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">trust--</hi>Greek, "to have their trust resting."<div eID="gen37496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37497" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in ... in--</hi>rather, "upon ... upon," as the oldest manuscripts.<div eID="gen37497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37498" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">uncertain riches--</hi>rather as Greek, "the uncertainty of riches." They who rest their trust on riches, rest trust on uncertainty itself (<reference osisRef="Prov.23.5">Pr 23:5</reference>). Now they belong to one person, now to another, and that which has many masters is possessed by none [Theodoret].<div eID="gen37498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37499" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">living God--</hi>The best manuscripts and versions omit "living." He who trusts in riches transfers to them the duty he owes to God [Calvin].<div eID="gen37499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37500" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">who giveth--</hi>Greek, "affordeth."<div eID="gen37500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37501" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all things richly--</hi>temporal and eternal, for the body and for the soul. In order to be truly rich, seek to be blessed of, and in, God (<reference osisRef="Prov.10.22">Pr 10:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.1.3">2Pe 1:3</reference>).<div eID="gen37501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37502" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to enjoy--</hi>Greek, "for enjoyment." Not that the heart may cleave to them as its idol and trust (<reference osisRef="1Tim.4.3">1Ti 4:3</reference>). Enjoyment consists in giving, not in holding fast. Non-employment should be far removed, as from man, so from his resources (<reference osisRef="Jas.5.2">Jas 5:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jas.5.3">3</reference>) [Bengel]. <div eID="gen37502" type="x-p"/>
entries.c0cfcfa5b17de59bb62b79d83314655d2d52e498: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18164"/><div sID="gen37503" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18164"/><hi type="bold">18. do good--</hi>like God Himself (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.68">Psa 119:68</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.14.17">Ac 14:17</reference>) and Christ (<reference osisRef="Acts.10.38">Ac 10:38</reference>). Tittmann translates, "to do," or "act well"; as the Greek for "to be beneficent" is a distinct word, agathopoiein.<div eID="gen37503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37504" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rich in good works--</hi>so "rich in faith," which produces good works (<reference osisRef="Jas.2.5">Jas 2:5</reference>). Contrasted with "rich in this world," <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.17">1Ti 6:17</reference>. Literally, it is "rich in honorable (right) works." Greek, "kalois," "ergois," are works good or right in themselves: "agathois," good to another.<div eID="gen37504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37505" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ready to distribute--</hi>free givers [Alford]; the heart not cleaving to possessions, but ready to impart to others.<div eID="gen37505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37506" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">willing to communicate--</hi>ready contributors [Alford]: liberal in admitting others to share our goods in common with ourselves (<reference osisRef="Gal.6.6">Ga 6:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.13.16">He 13:16</reference>). <div eID="gen37506" type="x-p"/>
entries.35d102686eaa252534a88ad8fe0212046ca2a513: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18165"/><div sID="gen37507" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18165"/><hi type="bold">19. Laying up in store--</hi>"therefrom (that is, by this means [Alford]; but Bengel makes the Greek "apo" mean laying apart against a future time), laying up for themselves as a treasure" [Alford] (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.19">Mt 6:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.6.20">20</reference>). This is a treasure which we act wisely in laying up in store, whereas the wisest thing we can do with earthly treasures is "to distribute" them and give others a share of them (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.18">1Ti 6:18</reference>).<div eID="gen37507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37508" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">good foundation--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.13">1Ti 3:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.6.48">Lu 6:48</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.11">1Co 3:11</reference>). The sure reversion of the future heavenly inheritance: earthly riches scattered in faith lay up in store a sure increase of heavenly riches. We gather by scattering (<reference osisRef="Prov.11.24">Pr 11:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.13.7">13:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.16.9">Lu 16:9</reference>).<div eID="gen37508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37509" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that ... eternal life--</hi>The oldest manuscripts and versions read, "that which is really life," its joys being solid and enduring (<reference osisRef="Ps.16.11">Psa 16:11</reference>). The life that now is cannot be called so, its goods being unsubstantial, and itself a vapor (<reference osisRef="Jas.4.14">Jas 4:14</reference>). "In order that ('with their feet so to speak on this foundation' [De Wette]) they may lay hold on that which is life indeed." <div eID="gen37509" type="x-p"/>
entries.d60c7710384864cd390793e6928039e81ceee042: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18166"/><div sID="gen37510" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18166"/>20-21. Recapitulatory conclusion: the main aim of the whole Epistle being here summarily stated.<div eID="gen37510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37511" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">O Timothy--</hi>a personal appeal, marking at once his affection for Timothy, and his prescience of the coming heresies.<div eID="gen37511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37512" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">keep--</hi>from spiritual thieves, and from enemies who will, while men sleep, sow tares amidst the good seed sown by the Son of man.<div eID="gen37512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37513" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that which is committed to thy trust--</hi>Greek, "the deposit" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.18">1Ti 1:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.12">2Ti 1:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.14">14</reference>; 2:2). "The true" or "sound doctrine" to be taught, as opposed to "the science falsely so called," which leads to "error concerning the faith" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.21">1Ti 6:21</reference>). "It is not thine: it is another's property with which thou hast been entrusted: Diminish it not at all" [Chrysostom]. "That which was entrusted to thee, not found by thee; which thou hast received, not invented; a matter not of genius, but of teaching; not of private usurpation, but of public tradition; a matter brought to thee, not put forth by thee, in which thou oughtest to be not an enlarger, but a guardian; not an originator, but a disciple; not leading, but following. 'Keep,' saith he, 'the deposit,'; preserve intact and inviolate the talent of the catholic faith. What has been entrusted to thee, let that same remain with thee; let that same be handed down by thee. Gold thou hast received, gold return. I should be sorry thou shouldest substitute aught else. I should be sorry that for gold thou shouldest substitute lead impudently, or brass fraudulently. I do not want the mere appearance of gold, but its actual reality. Not that there is to be no progress in religion in Christ's Church. Let there be so by all means, and the greatest progress; but then let it be real progress, not a change of the faith. Let the intelligence of the whole Church and its individual members increase exceedingly, provided it be only in its own kind, the doctrine being still the same. Let the religion of the soul resemble the growth of the body, which, though it develops its several parts in the progress of years, yet remains the same as it was essentially" [Vincentius Lirinensis, A.D. 434].<div eID="gen37513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37514" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">avoiding--</hi>"turning away from" (compare <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.4">2Ti 3:4</reference>). Even as they have "turned away from the truth" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.6">1Ti 1:6</reference>; 5:15; <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.4">2Ti 4:4</reference>).<div eID="gen37514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37515" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">profane--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Tim.4.7">1Ti 4:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.16">2Ti 2:16</reference>).<div eID="gen37515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37516" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">vain--</hi>Greek, "empty": mere "strifes of words," <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.4">1Ti 6:4</reference>, producing no moral fruit.<div eID="gen37516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37517" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">oppositions--</hi>dialectic antithesis of the false teachers [Alford]. Wiesinger, not so probably, "oppositions to the sound doctrine." I think it likely germs existed already of the heresy of dualistic oppositions, namely, between the good and evil principle, afterwards fully developed in Gnosticism. Contrast Paul's just antithesis (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.16">1Ti 3:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.5">6:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.6">6</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.15-2Tim.2.23">2Ti 2:15-23</reference>).<div eID="gen37517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37518" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">science falsely so called--</hi>where there is not faith, there is not knowledge [Chrysostom]. There was true "knowledge," a special gift of the Spirit, which was abused by some (<reference osisRef="1Cor.8.1">1Co 8:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.8">12:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.6">14:6</reference>). This gift was soon counterfeited by false teachers arrogating to themselves pre-eminently the gift (<reference osisRef="Col.2.8">Col 2:8</reference>, 18, 23). Hence arose the creeds of the Church, called symbols, that is, in Greek, "watchwords," or a test whereby the orthodox might distinguish one another in opposition to the heretical. Perhaps here, <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.20">1Ti 6:20</reference>, and <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.13">2Ti 1:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.14">14</reference>, imply the existence of some such brief formula of doctrine then existing in the Church; if so, we see a good reason for its not being written in Scripture, which is designed not to give dogmatic formularies, but to be the fountain whence all such formularies are to be drawn according to the exigencies of the several churches and ages. Probably thus a portion of the so-called apostle's creed may have had their sanction, and been preserved solely by tradition on this account. "The creed, handed down from the apostles, is not written on paper and with ink, but on fleshy tables of the heart" Jerome [Against John of Jerusalem, 9]. Thus, in the creed, contrary to the "oppositions" (the germs of which probably existed in the Church in Paul's latter days) whereby the aeons were set off in pairs, God is stated to be "the Father Almighty," or all-governing "maker of heaven and earth" [Bishop Hinds]. <div eID="gen37518" type="x-p"/>
